body: Spain uses standard long, white European plates with a single blue strip on the left. This distinguishes them from Portuguese plates (often with a yellow strip) and Italian plates (with two blue strips).
The standard Spanish bollard has a yellow-orange reflector on the front and two white dots on the back. A slightly different bollard, also used in Andorra, can be found near the border.
In rural Spain, concrete ladder poles and wooden poles are the most common types of electricity poles. 'Ladder' poles are recognizable by their ladder-like indents.
'French style' poletops, shaped like an upside-down triangle with a curved top bar, are common in Spain, often on ladder or steel poles. These are also very common in France.
High-voltage electricity pylons are a very common sight in Spain, more so than in other Mediterranean countries.
Spain has distinct road markers with a variety of colorful borders and a road number on top. The letter codes on these markers are important for region-guessing.

Rural Spain has two unique hunting signs: a white one with the words 'coto' and 'caza', and another with a diagonally divided black and white background. These signs may include a code indicating the region.
Spain uses yellow reflectors on rounded A-type guardrails. This feature is shared with Belgium, Andorra, and Gibraltar.
Spanish pedestrian crossing signs have 8 stripes, the highest number in Europe. This feature is only shared with Andorra.
Spanish stop signs feature a distinctively small font. This helps distinguish them from Portuguese stop signs, which use a larger font.
Red borders on Spanish road signs extend to the very edge, with no white border separating the red from the edge. This is a key difference from signs in France, Italy, and Portugal.
Most traffic signs, kilometre markers, and chevrons in Spain are mounted on a flat signpost. This type of signpost is also found in Portugal, France, and Andorra.
Spain uses two types of chevrons: black with white arrows and blue with white arrows. France is the only other European country with blue and white chevrons.
Spanish direction signs are white and often feature recognizable colorful boxes containing road numbers. Highway signs are blue.
Rural roads in Spain sometimes have dashed outer lines, a feature uncommon in Portugal and Italy.

The main language is Spanish, a Romance language. It can be distinguished from Portuguese by unique characters like Ñ, while Portuguese uses Ç and different word endings. Spain also has several regional languages like Catalan, Basque, and Galician.
The Spanish word for street is 'calle'.
'No parking' signs in front of garages often read 'Vado permanente' and frequently include the municipality's name. This is similar to Italy's 'Passo carrabile' signs.
Spain has a highly diverse landscape, from lush green forests in the north to dry semi-deserts. The terrain includes highland plateaus, rolling hills, and jagged mountains.
Most of Spain has a dry, Mediterranean climate with corresponding vegetation and agriculture.
Generation 3 coverage in Spain features cars with long, short, or no antennas. In some eastern regions, the long antenna has a distinctive white top.
Generation 4 cars in Spain are typically blue or sometimes black, and may be completely hidden.
Spain has some Generation 4 'smallcam' coverage, which is mounted lower and has a large, sometimes transparent, circular blur.
Spain has some low-quality 'Ari' or 'Shitcam' coverage, recognizable by a wide circular car blur, no sky halo, and often brownish colors.
Spanish regional road numbers feature region-specific codes on road markers and direction signs, which are very useful for region-guessing. National roads (E, AP, A, R, N) can be found anywhere.
Spanish area codes for landlines are very useful for region-guessing. Landline numbers start with a '9' followed by a regional code, while mobile numbers start with '6'.
Spain has several important regional languages, including Catalan, Basque, and Galician, which are very useful for region-guessing.
Catalan is spoken in Catalonia, Valencia, and the Balearic Islands. To distinguish it from Spanish, look for the word 'i' for 'and' (instead of 'y') and the common use of the grave accent (e.g., à).
The Catalan word for street is 'carrer'.
In Catalan-speaking areas, 'no parking' signs often read 'Gual permanent'.
Basque is a unique language isolate spoken in the Basque Country and northern Navarre. It has a distinct look with common letters like 'Z' and 'K'.
In Basque-speaking areas, the word for street is sometimes 'kalea'.
Road signs in the Basque Country and Navarre often feature distinctive bilingual sub-signs with a thick black border. The language order can help differentiate between the two regions.
Galician, spoken in Galicia, is closely related to Portuguese. It can be distinguished by the use of 'ñ' and the lack of 'ç'.
In Galicia, streets are commonly called 'Rúa', with an accent, distinguishing them from 'Rua' in Portugal.
Many Galician town names are unique for starting with articles like 'A', 'O', 'As', or 'Os'.
Learning the regional flags of Spain's autonomous communities is useful for region-guessing as they are reasonably common.
The unofficial Catalan Independence flag, featuring a blue triangle with a star over the red-and-yellow Senyera pattern, is common in Catalan-speaking areas.

Spain is a very mountainous country, with major ranges like the Pyrenees and the Baetic System. The center is dominated by the high, flat Meseta Central plateau, which is surrounded and crossed by other mountain ranges.
The far north of Spain has a much more green and lush landscape than the rest of the country, with hilly terrain, hedges, and green meadows.

The Pyrenees mountain range on the Spain-France border is known for light grey rock, abundant pine trees, and many rock walls. Andorra and the French Pyrenees have similar landscapes and architecture.
Thick pine forests are common throughout the Pyrenees; smaller pines between grazing fields are typical in the Basque Country and Navarra.
Castilla y León features a mostly flat agricultural landscape with cereal crops and common sunflower plantations.
La Rioja uniquely has vineyards between mountain ranges to the north and south.
A strip of semi-desert landscape spans Navarra and Aragón, with light sandy soil and small shrubs on hills around the Ebro river basin.
Aragón features very arid flat areas, with white rocky soil north and red soil in Teruel.
Castilla la Mancha has flat landscapes, vineyards, and western areas with olive tree plantations on flat terrain.
Open fields with holm and cork oaks are common in Extremadura and nearby, with more lush vegetation north of Cáceres.
The Murcia region is arid with sandy soil, medium mountains, and rural small shrubs and fruit/olive tree plantations.
Mountains around Murcia and south Alicante are rugged, sparsely vegetated, often with a hazy/misty look.
The Sierra Nevada mountain range has snowy peaks most of the year and is unique in southern Spain.
White houses built on mountain faces are typical around the south coast near Málaga.
Olive trees are a major crop and widespread across over half of Spain.
Around Córdoba and Jaén, vast olive tree plantations cover rolling hills, often in Generation 2 coverage.
South of Madrid, olive plantations grow in small to medium fields on flat terrain with red soil.
East coast olive plantations are fenced or behind rock walls, with mountains typically visible nearby.
Eucalyptus plantations dominate northern Spain’s coast, especially Galicia, and are also widespread in Portugal.
In dry environments, eucalyptus trees are mostly in Huelva province, and more rarely in Extremadura and towards Córdoba.
Orange tree plantations are found mostly in small valleys on Spain’s east coast, with mountains visible nearby.
Guadalquivir river basin has many orange plantations in flatter, more open terrain, with sparse mountainous coverage.
Corn is mainly grown in river basins, the north coast (Galicia), and northwest Castilla y León.
Stone pines have fluffy leaves and bulbous crowns; common around Valladolid, Huelva, and near Barcelona.
Aleppo pines are common on the east coast and Balearic Islands with fluffy leaves and less compact crowns.
Baltic pines are tall, thin, with dark bark revealing oranges underneath, found mainly in Pyrinees, Sierra de Guadarrama, and Iberian System.
Maritime pines near the Atlantic coast have grey bark with red undertones and upward branching; also common in Portugal.
The Mediterranean variant of maritime pines has fissured grey bark with red tones and grows in central/southern Spain and near Segovia.
Road lines are useful clues on small roads; regions favor either straight or dashed outer lines, with some provinces having unique patterns.
Spanish kilometre markers are mostly rectangular or square; unique tall markers exist in Andalusia, Madrid, Biscay, and national roads use red rectangles.
Markers have coloured borders (orange, green, yellow) by road size, with some regional variations.
Galician towns use signs with a green or blue strip at the top showing municipality names; 'Concello' is unique to Galicia.
Asturias bus stops often have a red post with CTA logo, which can be confused with Madrid’s red post stops managed by EMT.
Asturias has distinct trash containers with the COGERSA logo, also found on recycling bins.
Yellow snow poles with reflectors are unique to southern Asturias.
Aragón’s regional roads feature simple white rectangular bollards with grey reflectors common to that area.
Catalonia, the Basque Country, and Balearic Islands have round, corrugated signposts, especially for direction signs, similar to French designs.
Hunting signs in Catalonia and sometimes Balearic Islands read Àrea privada de Caça in Catalan.
A unique bollard, mostly in Lleida and Tarragona with an orange square reflector front and white reflector back, also seen in Canary Islands and some highways.
Catalonia features big square chevrons with single arrows.
Murcia is distinct with small square chevrons with red arrows on white.
Madrid region has red canopy bus stops and green buses, with urban centre using blue buses.
Spanish bollards with green tops are exclusive to Extremadura.
Castilla la Mancha features stone markers with the regional coat of arms lining fields, with blue left side and unpainted right.
Murcia and southern Alicante have poles with steel mesh rectangular structure instead of triangles.
Andalusian signs are recognizable by a green stripe on the left and green signposts near nature reserves.
Blue and yellow snow poles are unique to Andalusia.
Northwest Spain features predominantly slate roofs, especially in Galicia, Pyrenees near Andorra, and NE mountain ranges.
Many Galician houses are built with large concrete blocks, sometimes textured to look like natural stone.
Galicia has unique granaries called horreos gallegos or cabazos, made from various materials but with consistent shape.
Asturian hórreos are larger and square, often on four pillars; variations with slate roofs appear in western Asturias.
Large white houses with wooden frames are common in the Basque Country, Basque Navarra, and Cantabria.
Masías are traditional stone farmhouses common in Catalonia, eastern Aragón, and part of the Valencian Community.
In central and southern Spain, towns of entirely white painted houses are common in Andalucía and Extremadura.
Asturias has a distinctive black car with no antenna and visible brake light, rarely seen spilling into Galicia.
A special Generation 3 antenna with a white tip is found in eastern Andalusia and northeast provinces of Huesca and Lleida.
The Balearic Islands have a coastal Mediterranean look with dry Aleppo pine forests and small agricultural patches.
Low rock walls are very common in the Balearic Islands, similar to areas around Bari, Italy.
Typical Balearic houses are white, with flat or gently tiled roofs.
Grazing fields in the Balearic Islands are almost exclusive to Menorca.
Formentera island features low coastal shrubs and views of Ibiza’s mountains from its north coast.
Northwest Palma has tall mountains visible across the island, unique in the Balearics.
The Canary Islands are a Spanish archipelago off Africa’s west coast; recognizing them is crucial for mapping accuracy.
The Canaries have extremely diverse landscapes: steep mountains, pine forests, volcanic soil, and extreme aridity, often unlike mainland Europe.
Lanzarote features dark volcanic soil resembling the moon’s surface, the most common landscape of this type in the Canaries.
Fuerteventura has an arid landscape with orange soil, unique in the Canaries.
A unique bollard with a square orange reflector front and white reflector back is common in Las Palmas province and parts of mainland Spain.
Lanzarote’s vineyards are unique with volcanic soil and semicircle-shaped rock formations.
La Graciosa island off Lanzarote is barren with overcast weather and has two towns with white flat-roofed houses.
Spanish enclaves Ceuta and Melilla are in North Africa with coverage that may confuse new mappers.
Ceuta has North African architecture with flat, warm-colored houses and mostly sunny Generation 4 coverage.
Ceuta’s mountainous landscape features a mix of eucalyptus trees and pines.
Black and white guardrails are unique to Ceuta within Spain.
Melilla has similar North African architecture, appears hazier, has less saturated skies, mostly cloudy coverage, and limited rural areas near the Morocco border.
The Camino de Santiago pilgrimage routes across Europe are marked by a yellow scallop on blue on signs and waystones, often seeing hikers and bikers in summer.
Early spring coverage in central-north Castilla la Mancha shows dirt roads between green fields and leafless vineyards with red soil, mostly in Generation 3.
Navarra’s AP-15 highway features flat bollards with square red reflectors and guardrails with red reflectors.
Barcelona taxis are black with yellow doors, including the trunk.
The Ebro delta features an extremely flat landscape with rice fields and water canals, surrounded by significant mountains visible from most locations.
Near Almería and Motril, many white-roofed greenhouses are found in lowland coastal areas, especially in El Ejido.
Bilbao’s street signs have a uniquely elaborately decorated frame not found elsewhere in Spain.
A rare and unique car Meta appears in Doñana National Park, southwest of Seville.
